passages.t: The Rock, and how he carried his people
passages.happening:
The Song of Moses begins by calling its witnesses. “Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; hear, O earth, the words of my mouth” (verse 1). Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain on new grass (verse 2).

Then he names its subject. “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just. A God of faithfulness without injustice, righteous and upright is He” (verse 4).

Against that he sets the people. They have acted corruptly. “Is this how you repay the LORD, O foolish and senseless people? Is He not your Father and Creator?” (verse 6).

He tells them to remember the days of old (verse 7). God found Israel ‘in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness’. He ‘guarded him as the apple of His eye’ (verse 10). “As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, He spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions” (verse 11). He fed them with honey from the rock, with milk and wheat and wine (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
This is a song, and it should be read as poetry. Hebrew poetry is built in pairs of lines, in which the second line echoes or sharpens the first: ‘Let my teaching fall like rain and my speech settle like dew’.

Songs were how ancient peoples remembered. God told Moses in the last chapter to teach this one so that it would stay in Israel's mouth when everything else was forgotten.

The song has the shape of a case brought to court. Heaven and earth are called as witnesses. The faithfulness of the one who brings the case is declared. The ingratitude of the accused is described. A verdict follows. The prophets later used the same form.

God is called ‘the Rock’ five times in the song. In a land of cliffs and desert a rock meant shelter, defense and something that does not move. Everything else in the song shifts. The Rock does not.

Verse 6 calls God ‘your Father’, and it does so at the moment of Israel's ingratitude. A father is being repaid with contempt by the children he made.

Verses 8 and 9 look at all the nations. God, called ‘the Most High’, gave every people its place. And out of all of them he kept Israel as his own share. The note on chapter 4, verses 15 to 31, says more about the wording of verse 8, where old copies differ.

The two pictures in verses 10 and 11 are among the most tender in the Bible. ‘The apple of His eye’ speaks of something guarded as carefully as a person guards his own sight. And the eagle is pictured teaching its young to fly, hovering near and catching them on its wings when they fall. That is how the song remembers the forty years in the wilderness.
passages.later:
At Sinai God had used the same picture: ‘I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself’ (Exodus 19:4).

The psalms took up the song's name for God and its pictures. “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psalm 18:2). “Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings” (Psalm 17:8).

Isaiah opens his book as this song opens, with the same witnesses and the same charge: “Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the LORD has spoken: ‘I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me’” (Isaiah 1:2).
passages.asks: The song tells Israel to remember the days of old and to ask its elders. Ask who has told you the story of God's care in your own family or church, and whether you have asked. And think of the eagle. Ask whether there was a time when you were pushed out of a safe place and found, looking back, that you were caught.

passages.happening:
The song turns. “But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked”. He ‘abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation’ (verse 15). The people made God jealous with foreign gods. They sacrificed to ‘gods they had not known’ (verse 17). “You ignored the Rock who brought you forth; you forgot the God who gave you birth” (verse 18).

God saw it. He said, ‘I will hide My face from them; I will see what will be their end’ (verse 20). Because they provoked him with what is not a god, he will provoke them with ‘those who are not a people’ (verse 21). Fire, hunger, plague and the sword are named (verses 22-25).

Then God holds back. He would have made an end of them, he says, ‘if I had not dreaded the taunt of the enemy’, who would say, ‘Our own hand has prevailed; it was not the LORD who did all this’ (verses 26-27).

The song grieves. “If only they were wise, they would understand it” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel. It probably comes from a word meaning upright. Its use here is bitter. The upright one grew fat and kicked, like a well-fed animal that turns on its owner.

This is the warning of chapter 8 put into a song. The danger was never hunger. It was fullness. The gifts of verses 13 and 14 become the cause of the fall in verse 15.

In verse 18 God is pictured as a mother as well as a father. He ‘brought you forth’, and he ‘gave you birth’. The people have forgotten the one who bore them.

The judgments of verses 22 to 25 are fearful, and they fall on Israel. That is important for how the violent pictures of this song are read. The people being judged in these verses are God's own people. Other nations are not in view. And the one who sings it is Israel's own teacher.

Then the turn at verses 26 and 27. God stops short of destroying them. The reason given is his name among the nations. It is the argument Moses himself used when he prayed for Israel after the golden calf. The song shows God taking up the plea of his own servant.

Verse 21 looks further ahead than Israel could see. God will stir his people to jealousy by ‘those who are not a people’. Paul later read this of the nations coming to faith.

This song is in Israel's Scriptures because Israel kept it and sang it. Its hard words about Israel are a family's words about itself. They give no outsider a reason for contempt toward the Jewish people. The note on chapter 28, verses 15 to 46, says more.
passages.later:
Hosea heard God say what this song says about fullness: “When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me” (Hosea 13:6).

Paul quotes verse 21 when he writes about his own people and the nations: “I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation” (Romans 10:19). In the same letter he says that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1).

Paul uses the words of verse 5 as a description of the world in which Christians are to live honestly: ‘children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation’ (Philippians 2:15). He applies the song to the church's own conduct.
passages.asks: Jeshurun did not fall away in hard times. He fell away when he was full. Ask what your comfort has done to your prayers, your giving and your sense of needing God. And notice that the song asks Israel to sing about its own failure. Ask whether you can speak truthfully about your own.

passages.happening:
The song turns again, this time toward hope. God says, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (verse 35).

“For the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free” (verse 36). He will ask where the other gods are, the rocks in which people took refuge (verses 37-38).

Then God speaks of himself. “See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me. I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal, and there is no one who can deliver from My hand” (verse 39).

He swears to bring judgment on his enemies, in the language of sword and arrows (verses 40-42).

The song ends with a call to joy. “Rejoice, O heavens, with Him, and let all God’s angels worship Him. Rejoice, O nations, with His people” (verse 43). God will set things right, and ‘He will cleanse His land and His people’.
passages.hearers:
The moment of mercy is carefully placed. God acts ‘when He sees that their strength is gone’. Israel has nothing left to offer and no one left to help. That is when compassion comes. The song does not wait for Israel to deserve it.

The question of verses 37 and 38 is asked without cruelty. The gods to whom Israel gave its offerings are invited to stand up and help. They cannot.

Verse 39 is one of the great statements of the Old Testament about God. There is one God. Life and death are both in his hand. He wounds, and he also heals, and the healing comes last in the line.

In the Bible ‘vengeance’ is not private revenge. It is the act of a judge who restores justice. The song keeps it for God alone. Because it belongs to him, it does not belong to anyone else.

The last verse is a surprise. The song has been about Israel's sin and Israel's enemies, and it ends by inviting the nations to rejoice together with God's people. The story does not end with Israel alone, or with the nations shut out. Old copies of this verse differ in length, and the Berean Standard Bible follows the longer form found in a Dead Sea Scroll and in the old Greek translation.
passages.later:
Hannah sang the truth of verse 39 when God gave her a son: “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6).

Paul quotes verse 35 to tell Christians what they may not do: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

And he quotes the last verse to show that the good news was always meant for every people: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people” (Romans 15:10).

In the last book of the Bible those who have come through suffering sing ‘the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb’ (Revelation 15:3).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take a song about God's arrows and sword and vengeance?

The pictures in verses 23 to 25 and 41 to 42 are violent, and they can trouble a reader. Several things help.

First, this is poetry. It uses the stock pictures of ancient war to say how seriously God takes evil. And much of the violence in the song, the famine, the plague and the sword, falls on Israel itself as the judgment of the covenant. It does not fall only on outsiders.

Second, the song says that vengeance belongs to God so that it will not belong to people. The New Testament draws that conclusion directly, in Romans 12:19.

Third, the song ends in compassion. God vindicates his servants when their strength is gone, and the nations are called to rejoice.

Some readers stress that God's anger against evil is to be taken seriously and not softened. Others stress that language like this belongs to songs of grief and hope, and expresses trust that God will set things right. Both agree on this: the song gives no one permission for violence. It takes vengeance out of human hands.
passages.asks: The song says that vengeance is God's. Ask what wrong you are still holding on to because you want to see it paid back yourself, and what it would mean to hand it to the judge of all the earth. And read verse 36 again. Ask whether you believe that God comes near when your strength is gone.

passages.happening:
Moses, with Joshua beside him, recites the whole song in the hearing of the people (verse 44).

When he has finished he says, “Take to heart all these words I testify among you today, so that you may command your children to carefully follow all the words of this law. For they are not idle words to you, because they are your life, and by them you will live long in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess” (verses 46-47).
passages.hearers:
These are almost the last words of teaching that Moses gives. After this he will bless the tribes and climb the mountain.

He stands with Joshua. The old leader and the new one speak the song together, so that the people see that nothing changes in what they are to hear.

‘Take to heart’ is the language of chapter 6, where the words were to be on the heart before they were taught to children. Moses ends where he began. The words go inward first, and then to the next generation.

And he says what the words are. They are ‘not idle words’. God's law is not an extra, to be attended to when the real business of living is done. ‘They are your life.’ Moses said in chapter 30 that God himself is Israel's life. Here he says it of God's words. For Moses the two cannot be separated.
passages.later:
This book has said the same of the manna: man lives ‘on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD’ (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Jesus said of his own words what Moses says here: “The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life” (John 6:63).
passages.asks: Moses says that these words are not empty, and that they are life. Ask honestly which it is for you: whether Scripture is one interest among others, or something you could not live without. And ask what one sentence from this book you would most want the children you know to take to heart.

passages.happening:
“On that same day the LORD said to Moses, ‘Go up into the Abarim Range to Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab across from Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites as their own possession’” (verses 48-49).

“And there on the mountain that you climb, you will die and be gathered to your people, just as your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people” (verse 50).

God gives the reason. “For at the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, both of you broke faith with Me among the Israelites by failing to treat Me as holy in their presence” (verse 51).

“Although you shall see from a distance the land that I am giving the Israelites, you shall not enter it” (verse 52).
passages.hearers:
‘On that same day’. Moses has just finished the song, and the command to die comes at once.

The event God names is told in Numbers 20. The people had no water and turned on Moses. God told him to speak to the rock. Moses struck it, with angry words, and water came. God said then that Moses and Aaron had not trusted him enough to treat him as holy before the people.

Moses has spoken of this three times already in the book, each time saying that God was angry with him ‘on account of’ the people. Here God speaks, and names Moses' own act: ‘both of you broke faith with Me’. The two belong together. The people's quarreling pressed him, and what he did under that pressure was still his.

It is hard to read. Moses has served for forty years. He has carried this people, prayed for them when God would have destroyed them, and refused to be made great at their cost. And for one failure, at the end, he is kept out of the land he has been walking toward for a lifetime.

The book does not explain this away, and neither should a reader. Some point out that Moses stood before the whole nation as the one who spoke for God, and that what he did, he did in front of them all. Those who represent God to others are held to a strict account. Others note that Moses is shown sharing the lot of the generation he led, which also died outside the land.

Several things soften the scene without removing its grief. God does not send a messenger. He speaks to Moses himself. He tells him he will be ‘gathered to your people’, the same words used of Aaron's death. And he lets him see. The command is to go up and look. Moses will die with the promise before his eyes.

His exclusion from the land is not his exclusion from God. The last chapter will say that no prophet like him arose again, a man ‘whom the LORD knew face to face’.
passages.later:
Numbers records the original word: “Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them” (Numbers 20:12).

A psalm remembers it with sympathy for Moses: “At the waters of Meribah they angered the LORD, and trouble came to Moses because of them. For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips” (Psalm 106:32-33).

Another psalm says of Moses and Aaron together what this passage shows: “You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds” (Psalm 99:8).

And the Gospels record that Moses did at last stand in the land: “Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus” (Matthew 17:3).
passages.hard:
Why was Moses kept out of the land for one failure after a lifetime of faithful service?

Many readers feel that the judgment is severe, and the text does not ask them to feel otherwise.

The reason given is in verse 51. At Meribah, Moses and Aaron broke faith with God and did not treat him as holy before the people. Interpreters have understood this in several ways.

Some stress that the act was public. Moses was the leader and the one who stood between God and the people. He misrepresented God before the whole nation, and leaders are held to a higher standard.

Others note the stress, found elsewhere in this book, that Moses suffered partly on the people's account, bound up with the generation that died in the wilderness.

Others point out how the scene is softened. God himself shows Moses the land, God himself buries him, and he is honored above every later prophet.

Christian readers have often seen a further meaning. Even Moses, and the law he gave, could not bring the people into their final rest. The letter to the Hebrews develops that thought.

None of these answers takes away the grief of the scene. These notes do not choose among them.

It should be said plainly that this is the story of Moses. It is not a rule that God shuts people out for a single failure, and it is not a way to read any person's disappointments or losses. Moses died forgiven, honored and known by God.
passages.asks: Moses did not receive the thing he had worked toward all his life, and he was still God's servant to the end. Ask whether there is a hope you may not live to see fulfilled, and whether you can go on serving faithfully without it. And ask whether you measure God's love for you by whether you get what you long for.
